Reactive oxygen species generation induced by coupling Phanerochaete 
chrysosporium with intermittent micro-aeration to enhance 
methane production
Xuepeng Wang , Zhenru Wang , Ying Deng , Haohao Mao , Qilin Yu , Yaobin Zhang *
Dalian University of Technology School of Environmental Science and Technology No.2 Linggong Road, Ganjingzi District, Dalian, Liaoning 116024, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Reactive oxygen species
Intermittent micro-aeration
Oxidation-reduction potential
White-rot fungi
Lignocellulose
A B S T R A C T
Anaerobic digestion is constrained by the rate-limiting step of hydrolysis and acidogenesis of macromolecular 
organic matter, which significantly affects the overall process efficiency and system stability. This study intro­
duced aerobic fungi Phanerochaete chrysosporium into an anaerobic digestion system combined with intermittent 
micro-aeration to induce the generation of extracellular reactive oxygen species, thereby accelerating the 
decomposition of organic solid waste and promoting methane production. The results showed that under an 
optimal aeration intensity of 8 % (VAeration:VReactor)/day, the intermittent micro-aeration (IMA) group enhanced 
cumulative methane production by 17.22 %, while the combined application of IMA with P. chrysosporium (IMA- 
P) group increased by 26.36 %, both relative to the non-aerated control group lacking P. chrysosporium sup­
plementation. The implementation of intermittent micro-aeration induced periodic oscillations in oxidation- 
reduction potential, ranging from −460 mV to −300 mV, which subsequently triggered the generation of •OH 
at concentrations between 35.84 μM and 65.29 μM. Under the limited oxygen condition, P. chrysosporium 
secreted lignocellulolytic enzymes and enhanced •OH generation to accelerate the degradation of lignocellulose. 
Microbial community analysis revealed that P. chrysosporium could proliferate in the anaerobic digester under 
such intermittent micro-aeration conditions. The enrichment of methanogens capable of coping with O2 stress, 
along with the elevated abundance of antioxidant enzyme genes, might account for the effective continuation of 
methanogenesis under intermittent micro-aeration conditions. This study offered a feasible method to improve 
the anaerobic digestion of complex substrates through the combination of P. chrysosporium supplementation and 
intermittent micro-aeration.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion has been extensively employed as a sustainable 
biotechnology for resource recovery and energy generation from organic 
waste materials. However, the anaerobic digestion of solid organic 
wastes is constrained by the rate-limiting hydrolysis and acidogenesis 
stages, particularly in the degradation of recalcitrant lignocellulosic 
components [1]. The structural complexity and chemical stability of 
lignocellulose result in low biogas production efficiency, thereby 
significantly affecting the overall process efficiency and system stability 
[2].
White-rot fungi are specialized aerobic microorganisms that exhibit 
remarkable lignocellulose-degrading capacities through the production 
of extracellular oxidative enzymes [3,4]. Under aerobic conditions, they 
secrete ligninolytic enzymes such as laccase (Lac), manganese peroxi­
dase (MnP), and lignin peroxidase (LiP), which oxidize a wide range of 
substrates, including lignin, phenols, and other aromatic compounds 
[3,5]. Furthermore, the ligninolytic system of white-rot fungi generates 
reactive oxygen species (ROS), such as extracellular hydroxyl radicals 
(•OH), which effectively promote lignin degradation when ligninolytic 
enzymes cannot penetrate plant cell walls [6]. Specifically, the 
lignocellulose-oxidizing enzymes secreted by white-rot fungi catalyze 
the reduction of oxygen (O₂) to superoxide radicals (•O₂−), which un­
dergo dismutation to form hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) (•O₂−+ HO₂• +
H+ → O₂ + H₂O₂). Subsequently, H₂O₂ reacts with Fe(II) via Fenton-like 
reactions (Fe(II) + H₂O₂ → Fe(III) + •OH + OH−) to generate •OH [7,8]. 
As a potent oxidant with a high redox potential, •OH (an oxidation 
potential of 2.8 V vs. Standard Hydrogen Electrode) can disrupt the

complex structure of lignocellulose [9]. Extensive research has demon­
strated that white-rot fungi significantly enhance lignocellulose 
biodegradation and organic pollutant removal in aerobic systems 
[7,10]. These unique capabilities have led to their successful application 
in various biological processes, including aerobic composting processes 
for organic waste treatment and pre-treatment systems to improve the 
biodegradability of lignocellulosic materials prior to anaerobic digestion 
[4].
Traditionally, anaerobic digestion systems have been designed to 
exclude O₂ due to its inhibitory effects on obligate anaerobic microor­
ganisms such as methanogens. However, recent studies have demon­
strated that a controlled O₂ supply can enhance the anaerobic digestion 
performance of organic waste. For example, Fu et al. reported that 
intermittent aeration improved the cumulative methane yield and vol­
atile suspended solids (VS) removal rate of corn straw by 10.3 % and 
16.5 %, respectively [11]. In practice, air mixing replacing mechanical 
mixing has been a common strategy for enhancing organic solid waste 
treatment in biogas engineering [12,13]. Under optimal conditions, 
micro-aeration does not inhibit methanogens but improves process ef­
ficiency [11,14]. The enhanced performance is generally attributed to 
increased microbial diversity in anaerobic systems, accelerating the 
hydrolysis of complex organic matter [15,16].
Recent studies have revealed that introducing intermittent micro- 
aeration into anaerobic digestion systems can induce the generation of 
microbial extracellular ROS [17]. ROS are widely present in anoxic-oxic 
conditions, such as paddy soils, intertidal zones, and aerobic composting 
systems [18–20]. Specifically, under anaerobic conditions, microbial 
extracellular respiration transfers electrons to external electron accep­
tors (e.g., Fe(III)), generating Fe(II). In aerobic environments, O2 accepts 
electrons from microorganisms or Fe(II), producing ROS such as •O₂−
and H₂O₂, which then react with Fe(II) via Fenton-like reactions to 
generate •OH. These ROS, mediated by microorganisms under periodic 
anoxic-oxic conditions, play a critical role in substance transformation 
and cycling in natural ecosystems and engineered biosystems 
[17,21,22]. For instance, intermittent micro-aeration supply in anaer­
obic systems induced •OH generation, and enhanced the degradation of 
pharmaceuticals such as carbamazepine and sulfamethoxazole [17].
Considering that white-rot fungi can generate extracellular ROS, a 
result of extracellular O2 accepting the intracellular electron, it is 
reasonable to hypothesize that other extracellular electron acceptors 
such as electrodes or Fe oxides (ferrihydrite) with suitable oxidation- 
reduction potential (ORP) may substitute the extracellular O2 to main­
tain the metabolism of white-rot fungi under anaerobic conditions. The 
redox fluctuations induced by intermittent micro-aeration in anaerobic 
systems may allow white-rot fungi to proliferate and play a role in the 
anaerobic digestion of complex organic waste. However, rare research 
has been reported on white-rot fungi-enhanced micro-aerobic anaerobic 
digestion except for a recent study by Gong et al., who found that Pha­
nerochaete chrysosporium added to a micro-aerobic anaerobic digester 
could secrete Lac, MnP, and LiP to accelerate straw liquefaction and 
promote methane production [2]. However, whether white-rot fungi 
induce the generation of ROS in anaerobic digestion systems is un­
known. It is critical to elucidate the generation of ROS by white-rot fungi 
in oxygen-limited environments, which deepens the understanding of 
their role in complex organic matter degradation under natural and 
engineered biosystems.
This study aimed to accelerate lignocellulose degradation and 
enhance methane production by introducing white-rot fungi coupled 
with intermittent micro-aeration to induce the generation of ROS. 
P. chrysosporium was used here because it is commonly considered a 
model fungus for white rot fungi and is an efficient delignifier [23,24]. 
Particularly, this study was conducted to: (1) investigate the effects of 
white-rot fungi coupled with intermittent micro-aeration on anaerobic 
digestion; (2) analyze redox oscillations and ROS generation; and (3) 
determine the optimal aeration intensity for white-rot fungi prolifera­
tion through microbial community analysis.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Experimental materials
The inoculum sludge and cow manure were collected from an 
organic waste treatment company in Hangzhou. After being collected 
from a full-scale plant, the inoculum sludge was cultivated with cow 
manure as the substrate in a lab-scale semi-continuous reactor to 
maintain high methanogenic activity. The raw cow manure was stored 
at 4 ◦C before use to maintain its stable properties. The total suspended 
solids (TS) of the inoculum sludge were 19.35 g/L, and the VS was 6.03 
g/L. The TS of the cow manure was 35.51 g/L, and the VS was 26.80 g/L. 
P. chrysosporium was purchased from the Beina Biological Engineering 
and Technology Research Center and inoculated in potato dextrose agar 
medium at 30 
◦C. After culturing the spore suspensions of 
P. chrysosporium (OD600 = 1) for two week, the mycelium was harvested, 
dewatered via gauze filtration, and stored for subsequent experiments.
2.2. Batch experiment
The experiment was conducted in batch mode using 500 mL threa­
ded bottles. Three groups were conducted, i.e., the intermittent micro- 
aeration group (referred to as IMA group), the intermittent micro- 
aeration with P. chrysosporium addition group (referred to as IMA-P 
group), and the control group with no IMA and P. chrysosporium. Each 
group has three parallels. The experiment was run in three stages, each 
stage lasted for 36 days. At the beginning of each stage, 100 mL of 
inoculum (or digested liquid from the previous stage) was added, along 
with 350 mL of fresh cow manure (6 % solids content), and ferrihydrite 
(10 mM Fe(III)) was introduced as an iron source. Intermittent micro- 
aeration was performed daily by injecting a certain air volume into 
the reactors using a syringe, i.e., Stage 1 and 2: 20 mL/day (4 %(VAera­
tion:VReactor)/day), Stage 3: 40 mL/day (8 %(VAeration:VReactor)/day). The 
selection of the intensity of intermittent micro-aeration is detailed in 
Text S1. The IMA-P group only received an addition of P. chrysosporium 
mycelium (2 g wet weight/450 mL) at the start of the first stage. To 
avoid the influence of abiotic factors, the control and IMA groups were 
supplemented 
with 
an 
equivalent 
amount 
of 
inactivated 
P. chrysosporium mycelium. The prepared anaerobic bottles were placed 
in a constant-temperature incubator at 37 ◦C. During the experiment, 
sludge samples were collected using a syringe from rubber tubes 
equipped with valves, and the produced biogas was collected using gas 
bags.
2.3. ROS measurement
The •OH generation was determined by an electron paramagnetic 
resonance (EPR) spectrometer and quantified by coumarin, the H2O2 
was determined by cerium sulfate spectrophotometry as described in 
Text S2 [25,26].
2.4. Characterization and analysis
TS, VS, and biogas content and volume were analyzed as previously 
reported and detailed in Text S3. The capacitance and resistance of the 
sludge were determined according to the previous study and detailed in 
Text S4 [27].
Cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin were determined using the Alva 
semi-automatic crude fiber analyzer F1600 (Text S5). ORP and oxygen 
content in the headspace were evaluated by an ORP composite electrode 
(STARTER, 3100, USA) and a fiber-optic oxygen transmitter (FiBox3, 
PreSens, Regensburg, Germany), respectively. The activity of enzymes 
(Lac, LiP, and MnP) was quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent 
assay kits (Text S6).
The morphology of sludge after digestion was observed using a 
scanning electron microscope (SEM, HITACHI SU5000, China).

Functional groups of the sludge samples were evaluated by a Fourier- 
transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometer (ThermoFisher, 6700, Ger­
many) with a scanning range from 4000 to 400 cm−1. The composition 
of dissolved organic matter in the suspension was determined using a 
three-dimensional fluorescence spectrometer (Agilent, Cary Eclipse, 
Malaysia).
2.5. Microbial community analysis
The fungal community of sludge was analyzed via high-throughput 
sequencing by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd., China. The meta­
genomic analysis was conducted by Shanghai GeneCowin Biotechnology 
Co., Ltd., China. The detailed methods are provided in Text S7.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Performance of anaerobic digestion
Batch experiments with the control group, the intermittent micro- 
aeration (IMA) group and the intermittent micro-aeration with 
P. chrysosporium addition (IMA-P) group were conducted over three 
stages (3 × 36 days) under different aeration intensities. Ferrihydrite 
(10 mM Fe(III)) was added as an iron source at the beginning of each 
stage. The results demonstrated that P. chrysosporium coupled with 
intermittent micro-aeration effectively enhanced methane production 
from anaerobic digestion of organic solid waste. During stage 1–2 (0–72 
days), with an aeration intensity of 4 % (VAeration:VReactor)/day, the cu­
mulative methane production in the IMA group ranged from 126.35 to 
134.72 mL/gVS, 5.91 %–7.60 % higher than the control group 
(119.30–125.20 mL/gVS). In contrast, the IMA-P group exhibited higher 
cumulative methane production (126.61–141.50 mL/gVS), achieving a 
6.13 %–13.02 % enhancement over the control group (Fig. 1A). These 
results indicated that intermittent micro-aeration combined with 
P. chrysosporium addition promoted methane production.
Given the aerobic characteristics of P. chrysosporium, the limited 
oxygen supply might limit its activity. During stage 3 (72–108 days), the 
aeration intensity was adjusted to 8 % (VAeration:VReactor)/day. The IMA 
and IMA-P groups achieved cumulative methane production of 137.76 
mL/gVS and 148.57 mL/gVS, respectively, corresponding to a 17.22 % 
and 26.36 % increase over the control group (118.73 mL/gVS). Under 
similar operating conditions (25–39 ◦C), the specific methane produc­
tion obtained in this study was consistent with the literature range 
(49.54–409.76 mL/g VS) (Table S1). Moreover, the specific methane 
production in this work exceeded most of the previously reported 
values. Additionally, the methane production of the control group 
(118.73 mL/g VS) in stage 3 exhibited a slight decrease compared to the 
preceding two stages (119.30 mL/g VS, 125.20 mL/g VS, respectively), 
which might be attributed to the loss of functional microorganisms 
during substrate replacement in batch experiments. On the contrary, 
both the IMA and IMA-P groups displayed a consistent upward trend in 
methane production throughout stages 1 to 3. This result also indicated 
that both the IMA group and the IMA-P group demonstrated higher 
anaerobic digestion efficiency and greater stability in long-term 
operation.
Intermittent micro-aeration combined with P. chrysosporium addition 
improved organic substrate degradation. Sludge sampled on day 108 
was analyzed for waste reduction. As shown in Fig. 1B, the TS removal 
rate of the IMA group (43.06 %) and the IMA-P group (41.44 %) sur­
passed the control group (33.85 %) by 9.21 and 7.60 percentage points, 
respectively. Similarly, VS removal was enhanced in both micro- 
aeration groups. Additionally, cows digest the readily degradable por­
tions of feed (grass or silage) through rumen microbes, leaving cow 
manure with a fibrous nature. Specifically, the raw cow manure con­
tained 26.28 % ± 0.50 % hemicellulose, 29.41 % ± 0.67 % cellulose, 
and 14.07 % ± 1.14 % lignin in this study, respectively, consistent with 
the contents reported in the literature (Table S2). The complex struc­
tures of recalcitrant components (cellulose and lignin) in cow manure 
impede the hydrolysis process during anaerobic digestion [28,29]. After 
the treatment, the IMA-P group exhibited the lowest lignocellulose 
content at 60.71 % (hemicellulose: 26.27 %, cellulose: 23.83 %, lignin:

3.2. Redox oscillations and ROS generation
At an aeration intensity of 8 % (VAeration:VReactor)/day, ORP and 
headspace O2 contents were monitored. Results revealed that ORP 
rapidly increased to approximately −300 mV within 1 h after aeration, 
followed by a gradual decline to pre-aeration levels (about −460 mV). 
Concurrently, headspace O2 contents initially rose and declined after 
aeration (Fig. 2), indicating oxygen diffusion into the liquid phase and 
subsequent microbial consumption. The ORP fluctuations confirmed 
that intermittent micro-aeration induced redox oscillations in anaerobic 
digestion, creating favorable conditions for ROS generation [17].
Notably, P. chrysosporium accelerated oxygen utilization after aera­
tion. For example, ORP in the IMA group recovered to −429.5 mV (n =
4) 6 h after aeration, while the IMA-P group achieved a faster recovery to 
−461.25 mV (n = 4). This was corroborated by headspace O2 dynamics: 
O2 contents in the IMA-P group (0.542 % and 0.036 % at 3 h and 6 h, 
respectively) were significantly lower than those in the IMA group 
(0.912 % and 0.070 % at 3 h and 6 h, respectively) after aeration.
Redox oscillations typically induce ROS production [18,30]. To 
validate ROS generation triggered by intermittent micro-aeration, ROS 
quantification was conducted at peak oxidation-reduction potential (1 h 
post-aeration) within the bulk liquid phase. H₂O₂ was quantified using 
cerium sulfate spectrophotometry, and the results showed an average 
concentration of 24.19 ± 6.75 μM in the IMA-P group, 90.98 % higher 
than the IMA group (12.67 ± 3.78 μM), while the control group showed 
negligible detection (Fig. 3A).
Using DMPO (5,5-Dimethyl-1-Pyrroline-N-Oxide) as a spin-trapping 
agent to identify •OH, characteristic DMPO/•OH adduct signals (hy­
perfine coupling constants: αN = 14.89 G, αH
β = 14.89 G) were detected 
in both intermittent micro-aeration groups but not in the control 
(Fig. 3B). The DMPO/•OH signal intensity in the IMA-P group was 
significantly higher than that in the IMA group, indicating greater •OH 
production [31,32]. For quantitative analysis, 100 μM coumarin was 
added to the reactors to trap •OH and form 7-hydroxylcoumarin [33]. 
The results showed cumulative •OH levels within 1 h after micro- 
aeration in the IMA-P group was 65.29 ± 6.93 μM, 82.18 % higher

In this study, Ferrihydrite (10 mM Fe(III)) was added as the iron 
source into the anaerobic digestion system at the beginning of each 
cycle. During organic matter oxidation, Fe(III) could be reduced to Fe 
(II), which subsequently reacted with H2O2 to generate •OH through the 
Fenton-like reaction. Fe(II) content in the digested sludge was deter­
mined after 108 days of operation, and ranged from 212.7 ± 3.1 mg/L to 
296.9 ± 2.3 mg/L among the three groups. The presence of these Fe(II) 
species facilitated Fenton-like reactions to generate •OH within the 
intermittent micro-aeration system thereby improving the lignocellulose 
degradation capacity [9]. With P. chrysosporium addition, ROS produc­
tion in the intermittent micro-aeration system was significantly 
enhanced. The mechanism might involve H₂O₂ generation during 
P. chrysosporium metabolism, which served as a precursor for Fenton- 
like reactions and further promoted •OH production [8,34].
3.3. Ligninolytic enzyme activity
White-rot fungi possess a ligninolytic enzyme system capable of 
secreting Lac, MnP, and LiP, which can oxidize diverse substrates, 
including lignin, phenols, and other aromatic compounds. The activities 
of Lac, MnP, and LiP were analyzed using digestate samples collected 1 h 
post-aeration at an aeration intensity of 8 % (VAeration:VReactor)/day. 
Results showed negligible or minimal enzyme activity in the control 
group. In the IMA-P group, the activities of Lac, MnP, and LiP reached 
0.18 ± 0.05 U/L, 0.78 ± 0.27 U/L, and 0.69 ± 0.14 U/L, respectively, 
which were 112.80 %, 424.14 %, and 23.90 % higher than the IMA 
group (0.09 ± 0.04 U/L, 0.15 ± 0.12 U/L, 0.58 ± 0.13 U/L) (Fig. 4). 
Lac, MnP, and LiP synergistically oxidize aromatic structures in lignin, 
cleaving C-C and C-O bonds within lignin macromolecules, thereby 
facilitating lignin degradation [10,35]. These results demonstrated that 
P. chrysosporium addition enhanced lignocellulolytic enzyme activity in 
intermittent micro-aeration systems, accelerating lignocellulose break­
down, consistent with previous studies [2].
Lignocellulolytic enzymes can catalyze the reduction of O2 to H₂O₂, 
which induces Fenton-like reactions to produce •OH. The specific re­
action pathway is as follows: lignin-derived quinones (e.g., benzoqui­
none) are reduced to hydroquinones by quinone reductase. In the 
presence of lignocellulolytic enzymes, hydroquinones are oxidized to 
free semiquinone radicals, which undergo autoxidation to regenerate 
quinones while producing •O₂−. •O₂−
then disproportionate to form 
H₂O₂, ultimately generating •OH via Fenton-like reactions (Fig. S1) 
[5,7]. The significantly higher activities of ligninolytic enzymes in the 
IMA-P group compared to the IMA group facilitated •OH production and 
lignocellulose degradation, in agreement with the ROS and methane 
production.

3.4. Degradation of lignocellulose
Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) analysis revealed 
structural changes in lignocellulose within digestate samples collected 
on day 108 (Fig. 5A). The O-H stretching vibrations (3400–3200 cm−1) 
of lignin and cellulose showed intensified peaks in the IMA group and 
IMA-P group compared to the control group. It indicated that intermit­
tent micro-aeration decreased the association of O-H to induce lignin 
disruption, which was likely due to the attack of •OH [36]. The band at 
1600 cm−1 corresponding to aromatic ring stretching exhibited 
enhanced intensity in the IMA and IMA-P groups, suggesting destabili­
zation of aromatic frameworks and depolymerization of lignocellulose. 
These observations confirmed that P. chrysosporium coupled with 
intermittent micro-aeration promoted lignocellulose degradation. 
Furthermore, the increased C=O peak intensity at 1650 cm−1 (quinone 
groups) in the IMA and IMA-P digestates indicated quinone formation 
during lignocellulose degradation [37], which might facilitate extra­
cellular electron transfer via transformation of quinone/hydroquinones 
and ROS generation under the redox oscillations. Additionally, intensi­
fied C-O stretching/deformation bands (1300–800 cm−1) in the IMA and 
IMA-P groups reflected the enhancement of cellulose/hemicellulose 
degradation [38].
Three-dimensional excitation-emission matrix (3D-EEM) spectros­
copy further analyzed soluble organic components after the treatment. 
Elevated fluorescence intensities in the Ex/Em regions of 250–400/ 
380–500 nm (fulvic acid- and humic acid-like substances) were observed 
in the IMA and IMA-P groups compared to the control [39]. This indi­
cated the accelerated humification through the condensation of organic 
matter into macromolecular humic substances during the decomposition 
of lignocellulose.
3.5. Electrochemical activity
The combination of intermittent micro-aeration and P. chrysosporium 
supplement enhanced the electrochemical activity of microbial com­
munities. Cyclic voltammetry curves revealed that the sludge capaci­
tance in the IMA-P group and IMA group reached 2.04 × 10−4 F and 
1.84 × 10−4 F, respectively, which were 30.93 % and 17.70 % higher 
than the control group (1.56 × 10−4 F) (Fig. 6A). This suggested an 
increased availability of electron storage sites for microbial extracellular 
electron transfer [27]. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy results 
further showed that the sludge resistance in the IMA-P and IMA groups 
were 1138 Ω and 2000 Ω, respectively, which were 53.93 % and 19.03 
% lower than the control group (2470 Ω) (Fig. 6B). Lower resistance 
indicated the accelerated electron transfer within the sludge. Resistance 
and capacitance are commonly used indicators for evaluating extracel­
lular electron transfer in microbial communities [39–41]. These results 
demonstrated 
that 
intermittent 
micro-aeration 
coupled 
with 
P. chrysosporium addition improved microbial electrochemical activity, 
likely attributed to the generation of electroactive substances (e.g., 
quinones) during the humification of organic substrates.
3.6. Microbial community
3.6.1. Proliferation of fungi
To verify whether the exogenous P. chrysosporium proliferated in the

anaerobic system, the relative abundance of fungi in sludge was 
analyzed on days 36, 72, and 108. As shown in Fig. 7A, the relative 
abundance of P. chrysosporium in the fungal community reached 42.96 % 
at the end of the first stage (day 36). By the end of the second stage (day 
72), its abundance decreased from an initial 9.55 % (theoretical value: 
42.96 %/4.5, 4.5 representing the dilution by feeding) to 5.20 % under 
such intermittent micro-aeration (4 %(VAeration:VReactor)/day). However, 
during the third stage (days 72–108), as the aeration intensity increased 
from 4 % to 8 % (VAeration:VReactor)/day, the relative abundance of 
P. chrysosporium rose from an initial 1.16 % (theoretical value: 5.20 
%/4.5) to 1.54 %. In contrast, the relative abundance of P. chrysosporium 
in both the control group and IMA group was very low at the end of the 
operation on day 108 (<0.01 %). These results demonstrated that O2 
supply was critical for sustaining aerobic P. chrysosporium survival in 
anaerobic environments, and aeration intensity of 8 % (VAeration:VReac­
tor)/day could maintain its proliferation.
3.6.2. Enrichment of dissimilatory iron-reducing bacteria
The sludge collected from the reactors after 108 days of operation 
was analyzed through metagenomic analysis. Intermittent micro- 
aeration increased the diversity of the bacterial community (Table S3) 
and enriched dissimilatory iron-reducing bacteria (Fig. 7B), although

Longilinea, Petrimonas, Pseudomonas, Ralstonia, Sedimentibacter, Shewa­

group (2.37E+11copies/g) [42,43]. Intermittent micro-aeration can 
oxidize Fe(II) into Fe(III), thus providing a continuous Fe(III) source for 
the dissimilatory iron reduction (DIR) process, and enabling the 
enrichment of dissimilatory iron-reducing bacteria [44,45]. Meanwhile, 
the abundances of DIR-related genes in the sludge of the IMA group and 
the IMA-P group were distinctly upregulated compared with those in the 
control group (Fig. S3), which indicated an enhanced extracellular 
respiration capacity in the groups with intermittent micro-aeration 
[46–48]. This result was consistent with the enhancement of electro­
activity in the groups with intermittent micro-aeration.
3.6.3. Enrichment of methanogen
Intermittent micro-aeration increased the diversity of the bacterial 
community (Table S4). Methanothrix was identified as the predominant 
archaeal genus across all groups, demonstrating relative abundances of 
26.91 % in the control group, 22.03 % in the IMA group, and 21.35 % in 
the IMA-P group, respectively, showing a declining trend (Fig. S2B). 
However, the absolute abundances of Methanothrix in IMA group 
(2.46E+11 copies/g) and IMA-P group (2.22E+11 copies/g) were much 
higher than those in the control group (1.67E+11 copies/g), being 1.47 
times and 1.33 times that of the latter, respectively (Fig. 7C). Besides, as 
the methanogen genus with the second-highest relative abundance 
(4.06 %–4.79 %), Methanospirillum also had a higher absolute abun­
dance in the IMA group (4.55E+10 copies/g) and IMA-P group 
(4.98E+10 copies/g), compared to the control group (2.52E+10 copies/ 
g). This observed abundance of methanogens aligned with previous re­
ports demonstrating an O2 tolerance of both Methanothrix and Meth­
anospirillum, suggesting their crucial role in maintaining methanogenic 
activity under micro-aeration conditions [49,50]. In addition, the ROS 
induced by intermittent micro-aeration accelerated the decomposition 
of lignocellulose, which could provide more available substrates for 
methanogens [17,45]. This might be the reason why the abundance of 
methanogens is higher in the groups with intermittent micro-aeration.
3.7. Antioxidant defense mechanisms
It has been commonly acknowledged that aerobic bacteria possess 
antioxidant defense systems, which are capable of efficiently counter­
acting and reducing the detrimental impacts stemming from an over­
accumulation of ROS by synthesizing diverse antioxidant enzymes 
[51,52]. Conversely, obligate anaerobes do not have such a defense 
mechanism, making them unable to survive when exposed to oxidative 
stress [51,53]. Emerging research findings suggest that certain meth­
anogenic genera can cope with oxidative stress by encoding antioxidant 
enzymes that serve to detoxify the cellular environment [54,55]. How­
ever, the reports on the antioxidant mechanisms of anaerobic microor­
ganisms are still limited. In this study, the results of metagenomic 
analysis showed that the absolute abundance of superoxide oxide dis­
mutase, superoxide reductase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, perox­
iredoxins, and catalase-peroxidase were obvious higher in both the IMA 
groups and IMA-P group compared to the control group (Fig. 7D). 
Specifically, the total abundance of antioxidant enzymes in the IMA 
groups (2.40E+09 copies/g) and the IMA-P group (2.19E+09 copies/g) 
were 1.73 and 1.57 times that of the control group (1.39E+09 copies/g), 
respectively. This result indicated that domesticated anaerobic sludge 
by intermittent micro-aeration could effectively scavenge intracellular 
•O2
¡ and H2O2, protecting cells from oxidative stress damage [54].
The enrichment of methanogenic genera with the capacity to cope 
with O2 stress, along with the elevated abundance of antioxidant 
enzyme genes, might account for the effective continuation of meth­
anogenesis under intermittent micro-aeration conditions. This finding 
validated that the ability of anaerobic sludge to resist oxidative stress 
could be enhanced by O2 induction within the anaerobic digestion sys­
tem, which aligns with previous researches [45,54].
4. Conclusion
This study demonstrated that the P. chrysosporium supplementation 
coupled with intermittent micro-aeration induced ROS generation to 
accelerate organic solid waste decomposition and enhance methane 
production during anaerobic digestion. At an aeration of 8 % (VAeration: 
VReactor)/day, the IMA and IMA-P groups achieved 17.22 % and 26.36 % 
higher methane production compared to the control, alongside the 
improvement of TS and VS removal. Intermittent micro-aeration trig­
gered periodic redox oscillations to generate ROS. Under oxygen-limited 
conditions, P. chrysosporium secreted lignocellulolytic enzymes and 
enhanced •OH generation to accelerate lignocellulose degradation. 
Microbial community analysis confirmed P. chrysosporium proliferation 
in the intermittent micro-aerobic anaerobic system at an aeration in­
tensity of 8 % (VAeration:VReactor)/day. This study elucidated the ROS- 
mediated enhancement of anaerobic digestion of organic solid waste 
by coupling P. chrysosporium supplementation with intermittent micro- 
aeration, providing novel insights for advancing micro-aerobic anaer­
obic digestion technology in engineering applications.
